caption: Figure1Overview of WaltzRL. Left: Given a user prompt, the conversation agent produces an initial response. The feedback agent then reasons about its safety and overrefusal, produces labels, and a textual feedback. If the initial response is deemed unsafe or overrefusing according to the label, the feedback is given to the conversation agent which produces a revised response. Here, the feedback agent converts an unsafe response into a safe, balanced response to an adversarial prompt (detailed in §G). Right: A single training step of WaltzRL. After collaborative rollout, we gather training samples, compute the reward separately for each agent, and train both agents in parallel.

-Agent Reinforcement Learning Overview of a single training step of WaltzRL We update both the conversation and feedback agents in each step of WaltzRL (Alg. 1). This enables step-level co-adaptation between the two agents. (I) In each RL step, we first produce collaborative rollouts through multi-turn, multi-agent interactions. Figure 2 Left: Rate of conversation agent responses that improve under feedback in three setups (see ( §3.3). Middle: Rate of conversation agent response that has worsened under feedback. Right: Accuracy of feedback agent predicted (unsafe, overrefuse) labels.

Self-play and multi-agent RL Closely related to our work,<ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Liu et al. (2025)</ref> cast a single model into attacker and defender roles and conducts a zero-sum game to train both roles through RL.<ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Zhou et al. (2025)</ref> trains LLM agents that interact with a human collaborator over multiple turns.<ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Zha et al. (2025)</ref> and Sareen et al. (2025) train LLM for both generator and verifier roles to enhance reasoning capabilities. Recent works have formulated alignment as a two-player game but only explored zero-sum settings where higher reward of one agent leads to lower reward of the other one<ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Zheng et al., 2024;</ref><ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Ye et al., 2025)</ref>. We differ from prior work in that: (1) We deploy both agents at inference time, whereas<ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Liu et al. (2025)</ref>;<ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Zheng et al. (2024)</ref> only deploy the trained defender LLM. (2) Our positive-sum reward setting explicitly encourages collaboration between agents.

Figure 3 Stage 1 training dynamics. Left: Change of label correctness rate during stage 1 training. Right: Change of JSON parsing error rate during stage 1 training. The feedback agent learns the correct label and format in the first stage.

Figure 4 Stage 2 training dynamics. Left: Reward of initial conversation agent response c0. Right: Outcome reward of the final conversation agent response. WaltzRL successfully enhance the reward of both the initial response and the final outcome.
